They are centered at the sample mean and correspond to one and two standard deviations, respectively.
The covariance ellipses illustrate three important aspects of the covariance matrix:

The center of each ellipse is the mean vector.
The lengths of the major and minor axes are proportional to the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{X})\), reflecting the variability in the principal directions of the data.
The orientation of the ellipse is determined by the eigenvectors of \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{X})\). If the variables are uncorrelated, the ellipse is aligned with the coordinate axes; otherwise, it is rotated.



Show Python code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)


def add_covariance_ellipse(
    ax,
    mean,
    covariance,
    standard_deviations=1,
    **kwargs
):
    """Draw a covariance ellipse."""

    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covariance)

    order = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1]
    eigenvalues = eigenvalues[order]
    eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, order]

    angle = np.degrees(
        np.arctan2(
            eigenvectors[1, 0],
            eigenvectors[0, 0]
        )
    )

    width = (
        2
        * standard_deviations
        * np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0])
    )

    height = (
        2
        * standard_deviations
        * np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1])
    )

    ellipse = Ellipse(
        xy=mean,
        width=width,
        height=height,
        angle=angle,
        fill=False,
        **kwargs
    )

    ax.add_patch(ellipse)


# ==========================================================
# Correlated random vector (mixture)
# ==========================================================

sample_size = 2500

first_probability = 0.65
second_probability = 0.35

first_mean = np.array([-2.0, -1.0])
second_mean = np.array([3.0, 2.0])

first_covariance = np.array([
    [0.7, 0.25],
    [0.25, 0.6]
])

second_covariance = np.array([
    [0.8, -0.2],
    [-0.2, 0.7]
])

mixture_component = rng.binomial(
    n=1,
    p=second_probability,
    size=sample_size
)

first_cluster = rng.multivariate_normal(
    mean=first_mean,
    cov=first_covariance,
    size=sample_size
)

second_cluster = rng.multivariate_normal(
    mean=second_mean,
    cov=second_covariance,
    size=sample_size
)

sample = np.where(
    mixture_component[:, None] == 1,
    second_cluster,
    first_cluster
)

theoretical_mean = (
    first_probability * first_mean
    + second_probability * second_mean
)

empirical_mean = sample.mean(axis=0)

empirical_covariance = np.cov(
    sample,
    rowvar=False
)

# ==========================================================
# Independent random vector
# ==========================================================

independent_mean = np.array([0.5, 0.5])

# Different variances but zero covariance
independent_covariance = np.array([
    [2.0, 0.0],
    [0.0, 0.5]
])

independent_sample = rng.multivariate_normal(
    mean=independent_mean,
    cov=independent_covariance,
    size=sample_size
)

independent_empirical_mean = independent_sample.mean(axis=0)

independent_empirical_covariance = np.cov(
    independent_sample,
    rowvar=False
)

# ==========================================================
# Plot
# ==========================================================

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    1,
    2,
    figsize=(14, 6),
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

datasets = [
    {
        "sample": sample,
        "mean": theoretical_mean,
        "sample_mean": empirical_mean,
        "covariance": empirical_covariance,
        "title": "Correlated Components"
    },
    {
        "sample": independent_sample,
        "mean": independent_mean,
        "sample_mean": independent_empirical_mean,
        "covariance": independent_empirical_covariance,
        "title": "Independent Components"
    }
]

for ax, data in zip(axes, datasets):

    ax.scatter(
        data["sample"][:, 0],
        data["sample"][:, 1],
        s=12,
        alpha=0.25,
        label="Observations"
    )

    ax.scatter(
        data["mean"][0],
        data["mean"][1],
        marker="X",
        s=180,
        edgecolors="black",
        linewidths=1,
        label=r"$E[\mathbf{X}]$",
        zorder=5
    )

    ax.scatter(
        data["sample_mean"][0],
        data["sample_mean"][1],
        marker="P",
        s=130,
        edgecolors="black",
        linewidths=1,
        label=r"$\overline{\mathbf{X}}$",
        zorder=5
    )

    add_covariance_ellipse(
        ax,
        data["sample_mean"],
        data["covariance"],
        standard_deviations=1,
        linewidth=2.2,
        linestyle="--",
        label=r"$1\sigma$ ellipse"
    )

    add_covariance_ellipse(
        ax,
        data["sample_mean"],
        data["covariance"],
        standard_deviations=2,
        linewidth=2.2,
        linestyle=":",

    )

    ax.annotate(

        xy=data["mean"],

            arrowstyle="->",

    covariance_text = (

        f" [{data['covariance'][1,0]:.2f}, {data['covariance'][1,1]:.2f}]]"

    ax.text(

    ax.axhline(

    )

    ax.axvline(

    )

    ax.set_title(
        data["title"],

    )

    ax.set_xlabel("$X$")

axes[0].set_ylabel("$Y$")

title: Seminar 9: Expectation. Moment Generating Functions
text:
The standard Cauchy distribution has density
\[
f(x)
=
\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)},
\qquad
-\infty<x<\infty.
\]
Its expectation is
\[
E[X]
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)}
\,dx.
\]
However,
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{|x|}{\pi(1+x^2)}
\,dx
=
\infty.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
E[X]\ \text{does not exist.}
}
\]

title: Seminar 9: Expectation. Moment Generating Functions
text:
Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with density \(p(x)\), and let \(g\) be any continuous function.
Then
\[
\boxed{
E[g(X)]
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
g(x)\,p(x)\,dx.
}
\]
This formula allows us to compute expectations without first finding the distribution of \(g(X)\).

title: Seminar 9: Expectation. Moment Generating Functions
text:
2.1 Taylor Expansion
The exponential function has the Taylor expansion
\[
e^{tX}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\frac{(tX)^k}{k!}.
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_X(t)
&=
\mathbb E[e^{tX}]\\
&=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\frac{t^k}{k!}
\mathbb E[X^k].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the coefficients of the Taylor series are precisely the moments of the distribution.


Show Python code
mu = 1
sigma = 1.2

t = np.linspace(-0.8, 0.8, 1000)

mgf = np.exp(
    mu * t
    + sigma**2 * t**2 / 2
)

first_moment = mu

second_moment = (
    mu**2 + sigma**2
)

linear_approximation = (
    1 + first_moment * t
)

quadratic_approximation = (
    1
    + first_moment * t
    + second_moment * t**2 / 2
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

ax.plot(
    t,
    mgf,
    linewidth=2.6,
    label=r"$M_X(t)$"
)

ax.plot(
    t,
    linear_approximation,
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=2,
    label=r"$1+E[X]t$"
)

ax.plot(
    t,
    quadratic_approximation,
    linestyle=":",
    linewidth=2.5,
    label=r"$1+E[X]t+\frac{E[X^2]}{2}t^2$"
)

ax.scatter(
    0,
    1,
    s=60,
    edgecolor="black",
    linewidth=1,
    zorder=4
)

ax.annotate(
    r"$M_X(0)=1$",
    xy=(0, 1),
    xytext=(-0.65, 2.2),
    arrowprops={
        "arrowstyle": "->"
    }
)

ax.set(
    xlabel="$t$",
    ylabel="$M_X(t)$",
    title=(
        r"MGF and Its Taylor Expansion Near $t=0$"
        + "\n"
        + rf"$M_X'(0)=E[X]={first_moment:.2f}$, "
        + rf"$M_X''(0)=E[X^2]={second_moment:.2f}$"
    )
)

ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Seminar 9: Expectation. Moment Generating Functions
text:
2.2 Existence
Unlike expectations, moment generating functions do not always exist.
The expectation \(\mathbb E[e^{tX}]\) must be finite.
Some heavy-tailed distributions do not possess a finite moment generating function for any nonzero value of \(t\).

title: Seminar 9: Expectation. Moment Generating Functions
text:
2.3 Uniqueness Theorem
One of the most important theoretical results states that

If two random variables have the same moment generating function on an open interval containing zero, then they have exactly the same probability distribution.

Therefore,
\[
M_X(t)=M_Y(t)
\quad
\Longrightarrow
\quad
X\overset{d}=Y.
\]
This theorem makes the MGF an extremely useful tool for identifying probability distributions.

title: Seminar 9: Expectation. Moment Generating Functions
text:
2.4 Properties

Computing Moments
\[
M_X^{(k)}(0)=\mathbb E[X^k],
\qquad k=1,2,\ldots
\]
In particular, \(\mathbb E[X]=M_X'(0)\).
Sum of Independent Random Variables
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then
\[
M_{X+Y}(t)=M_X(t)M_Y(t).
\]
More generally, if \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent, then
\[
M_{X_1+\cdots+X_n}(t)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n} M_{X_i}(t).
\]

Distribution


Parameters


Moment Generating Function






Bernoulli


\(X\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\)


\(M_X(t)=1-p+pe^t\)




Binomial


\(X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)\)


\(M_X(t)=\left(1-p+pe^t\right)^n\)




Geometric


\(X\sim\mathrm{Geometric}(p)\)


\(M_X(t)=\dfrac{pe^t}{1-(1-p)e^t}\)




Negative Binomial


\(X\sim\mathrm{NegBin}(r,p)\)


\(M_X(t)=\left(\dfrac{pe^t}{1-(1-p)e^t}\right)^r\)




Poisson


\(X\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\)


\(M_X(t)=\exp\!\left(\lambda(e^t-1)\right)\)




Uniform


\(X\sim U(a,b)\)


\(M_X(t)=\dfrac{e^{tb}-e^{ta}}{t(b-a)}\)




Exponential


\(X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\)


\(M_X(t)=\dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}\)




Gamma


\(X\sim\Gamma(\alpha,\lambda)\)


\(M_X(t)=\left(\dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}\right)^\alpha\)




Normal


\(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\)


\(M_X(t)=\exp\!\left(\mu t+\dfrac{\sigma^2t^2}{2}\right)\)






For the Geometric distribution,
\[
\mathbb P(X=k)=p(1-p)^{k-1},
\qquad
k=1,2,\ldots
\]
For the Exponential and Gamma distributions, the formulas are valid for
\[
t<\lambda.
\]

title: Seminar 9: Expectation. Moment Generating Functions
section: 2.7 Why Do We Care About MGFs?
text:
2.7 Why Do We Care About MGFs?
At first glance, the moment generating function (MGF) may seem like just another way to describe a probability distribution. However, it is one of the most useful tools in probability theory.
First, the MGF provides a convenient way to compute the moments of a random variable.
Even more importantly, MGFs play a central role in proving fundamental results about sums of independent random variables. In particular, they provide one of the simplest and most elegant proofs of the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) one of the most important results in probability and statistics.

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
A discrete random variable assigns positive probability to countably many values.
A continuous random variable distributes its probability over intervals rather than individual points. In this lecture we study the most important class of continuous distributions: absolutely continuous distributions.

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
1.1 Cumulative Distribution Function
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a random variable \(\xi\) is defined by
\[
F_{\xi}(x)=P(\xi\le x),\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
\]
Notice that the CDF completely determines the probability distribution.
In other words, if two random variables have the same cumulative distribution function, then they have the same distribution.

1.1.1 Properties of the CDF

\(F(x)\) is non-decreasing.
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1\).
\(F(x)\) is right-continuous.



Show Python code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm

x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 1000)
F = norm.cdf(x)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.8))

# =====================================================
# (1) Monotonicity
# =====================================================

ax = axes[0]

ax.plot(x, F, linewidth=3)
ax.set_title("Monotonicity")

for x0 in [-2.5, -1, 0.5]:
    ax.annotate(
        "",
        xy=(x0 + 0.7, norm.cdf(x0 + 0.7)),
        xytext=(x0, norm.cdf(x0)),
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2)
    )

ax.text(
    -3.7,
    0.9,
    "F(x) is non-decreasing",
    fontsize=12,
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", fc="white")
)

ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("F(x)")
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

# =====================================================
# (2) Limits
# =====================================================

ax = axes[1]

ax.plot(x, F, linewidth=3)

ax.axhline(0, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)
ax.axhline(1, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)

ax.text(-3.8, 0.04, "As x -> -infinity, F(x) -> 0", fontsize=11)
ax.text(-3.8, 0.95, "As x -> infinity, F(x) -> 1", fontsize=11)

ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)
ax.set_title("Limits")
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

# =====================================================
# (3) Right continuity
# =====================================================

ax = axes[2]

x0 = 1.0

x_left = np.linspace(-3, x0, 400, endpoint=False)
x_right = np.linspace(x0, 3, 400)

F_left = 0.15 + 0.45 / (1 + np.exp(-2 * x_left))
F_right = 0.80 + 0.18 * (1 - np.exp(-(x_right - x0)))

left_limit = F_left[-1]
right_value = F_right[0]

ax.plot(x_left, F_left, linewidth=3)
ax.plot(x_right, F_right, linewidth=3)

# Open circle: left limit
ax.plot(
    x0,
    left_limit,
    marker="o",
    markersize=10,
    markerfacecolor="white",
    markeredgewidth=2
)

# Filled circle: actual value F(x0)
ax.plot(
    x0,
    right_value,
    marker="o",
    markersize=10
)

# Jump line
ax.vlines(
    x0,
    left_limit,
    right_value,
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=2
)

ax.annotate(
    "Right continuity:\nF(x0) equals the\nright-hand limit",
    xy=(x0, right_value),
    xytext=(1.35, 0.45),
    fontsize=11,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2),
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc="white", ec="gray")
)

ax.text(
    x0 - 0.9,
    left_limit - 0.08,
    "left limit",
    fontsize=10
)

ax.text(
    x0 + 0.08,
    right_value + 0.03,
    "F(x0)",
    fontsize=10
)

ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3)
ax.set_title("Right continuity")
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

plt.suptitle(
    "Three Fundamental Properties of a Cumulative Distribution Function",
    fontsize=16
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









There are three fundamentally different types of probability distributions:

Discrete distributions;
Singular distributions;
Absolutely continuous distributions.

Moreover, every probability distribution can be uniquely decomposed into a mixture of these three types.
A singular distribution is concentrated on an uncountable set of Lebesgue measure zero, while assigning probability zero to every individual point.
The most famous example is the Cantor distribution, whose cumulative distribution function is known as the Devil’s staircase.
In this course we will only study discrete and absolutely continuous distributions.

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
1.2 Discrete Probability Distributions
A probability distribution is called discrete if there exists a finite or countable set
\[
X=\{x_1,x_2,\ldots\}\subset\mathbb R
\]
such that \(P(X)=1\).

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
1.3 Example 1: Bernoulli Distribution
Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\). Its cumulative distribution function is
\[
F(x)=
\begin{cases}
0,&x<0,\\[1ex]
1-p,&0\le x<1,\\[1ex]
1,&x\ge1.
\end{cases}
\]
Notice that the CDF is a step function with jumps equal to the probabilities of the corresponding outcomes.


Show Python code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

p = 1 / 3

x_values = np.array([0, 1])
pmf = np.array([1 - p, p])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))

# =========================
# PMF
# =========================

ax = axes[0]

ax.vlines(x_values, 0, pmf, linewidth=4)
ax.scatter(x_values, pmf, s=90, zorder=3)

ax.set_xticks([0, 1])
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)

ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("p(x)")
ax.set_title("PMF of Bernoulli(1/3)")

ax.text(0.05, 1 - p + 0.03, "2/3", fontsize=12)
ax.text(1.05, p + 0.03, "1/3", fontsize=12)

ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

# =========================
# CDF
# =========================

ax = axes[1]

# Horizontal pieces of the CDF
ax.hlines(0, -0.5, 0, linewidth=3)
ax.hlines(1 - p, 0, 1, linewidth=3)
ax.hlines(1, 1, 1.5, linewidth=3)

# Open circles: left limits
ax.scatter(
    [0, 1],
    [0, 1 - p],
    s=80,
    facecolors="white",
    edgecolors="black",
    linewidth=2,
    zorder=5
)

# Closed circles: actual CDF values
ax.scatter([0, 1], [1 - p, 1], s=80, zorder=6)

# Vertical jumps
ax.vlines(0, 0, 1 - p, linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
ax.vlines(1, 1 - p, 1, linestyle="--", linewidth=2)

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 1.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)

ax.set_xticks([0, 1])
ax.set_yticks([0, 1 - p, 1])
ax.set_yticklabels(["0", "2/3", "1"])

ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("F(x)")
ax.set_title("CDF of Bernoulli(1/3)")

ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

plt.suptitle("Bernoulli Distribution with p = 1/3", fontsize=15)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
section: 2.1 Properties of the Probability Density Function
text:
2.1 Properties of the Probability Density Function

If the cumulative distribution function is differentiable, then

\[
p(x)=F'(x).
\]

Every probability density function integrates to one,

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(x)\,dx=1.
\]

The probability of any Borel set \(B\subseteq\mathbb R\) is obtained by integrating the density over that set,

\[
P(B)=\int_B p(t)\,dt.
\]
In particular,
\[
P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b p(t)\,dt.
\]

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
2.2 Examples of Absolutely Continuous Distributions

2.2.1 Uniform Distribution
Let $ XU([a,b])$, where \(a<b\). The probability density function is
\[
p(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac1{b-a},&a\le x\le b,\\[1ex]
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Every interval of the same length inside \([a,b]\) has the same probability.


Show Python code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import uniform

# Parameters
a = 2
b = 6
n = 20_000

# Simulated sample
sample = np.random.uniform(a, b, size=n)

# Theoretical curves
x = np.linspace(a - 1, b + 1, 1000)
pdf = uniform.pdf(x, loc=a, scale=b - a)
cdf = uniform.cdf(x, loc=a, scale=b - a)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

# =====================================================
# PDF
# =====================================================

ax = axes[0]

ax.hist(
    sample,
    bins=40,
    density=True,
    alpha=0.65,
    label="Simulated data"
)

ax.plot(
    x,
    pdf,
    linewidth=3,
    label="Theoretical PDF"
)

ax.set_title("Uniform Distribution: PDF")
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
ax.legend()

# =====================================================
# CDF
# =====================================================

ax = axes[1]

ax.plot(
    x,

2.2.2 Exponential Distribution
Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), where \(\lambda>0\). Its probability density function is
\[
p(x)=
\begin{cases}
\lambda e^{-\lambda x},&x\ge0,\\[1ex]
0,&x<0.
\end{cases}
\]
The exponential distribution is commonly used to model waiting times.

2.2.3 Normal Distribution
A random variable is said to follow a normal distribution with parameters \(\mu\in\mathbb R\) and \(\sigma^2>0\), if its probability density function is
\[
p(x)=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}
\exp\!\left(
-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}
\right).
\]
We write
\[
\boxed{
X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)
}
\]

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
2.3 The Standard Normal Table
The cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution, \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), is denoted by
\[
\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z).
\]
Unlike the cumulative distribution functions of the uniform or exponential distributions, the integral
\[
\Phi(z)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{-\infty}^{z}
e^{-t^2/2}\,dt
\]
cannot be evaluated using elementary functions.
For this reason, values of \(\Phi(z)\) are usually obtained from a standard normal table, often called the Z-table.

2.3.1 How is the Z-table organized?
The Z-table contains numerical values of \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\) for many values of \(z\).
Typically,

the row contains the first decimal digit of \(z\);
the column contains the second decimal digit.

Suppose we want to compute \(P(Z\le1.23)\). Looking up the entry corresponding to row 1.2, and column 0.03, we obtain approximately
\[
\boxed{\Phi(1.23)\approx0.8907.}
\]
Therefore,
\[
P(N(0,1)\le1.23)\approx0.8907.
\]


Show Python code

section: 2.4 Why is the normal distribution so important?
text:
2.4 Why is the normal distribution so important?
Many real-world variables are approximately normally distributed. Human heights, standardized test scores, measurement errors, IQ scores, and many biological characteristics often follow a distribution that is remarkably close to a normal distribution. Even when the data are not perfectly normal, the normal distribution frequently provides an excellent approximation.
In the examples below, we compare two real datasets:

Data Science salaries (Worldwide, 2023) — the distribution is noticeably right-skewed because a small number of very highly paid professionals earn much more than the majority.
NHANES adult heights (United States, 2017–2020) — the distribution is very close to a normal distribution, as predicted by many biological models.

The histograms and QQ-plots clearly illustrate this contrast. While salaries deviate substantially from normality, human heights closely follow a bell-shaped curve, making the normal distribution an excellent model.
This is one of the main reasons why the normal distribution plays such a central role in probability and statistics. In later seminars, we will see that many statistical methods—including confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, linear regression, and the Central Limit Theorem—are built upon the remarkable mathematical properties of the normal distribution.

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
3.1 The Inverse Transform Method
Let \(U\sim U(0,1)\) and let \(F\) be the CDF of a continuous random variable. Define
\[
X=F^{-1}(U).
\]
Then \(X\) has CDF \(F\). Indeed, for any \(x\),
\[
P(X\le x)
=
P(F^{-1}(U)\le x)
=
P(U\le F(x))
=
F(x),
\]
because \(U\) is uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\).
Thus, \(X=F^{-1}(U)\) transforms uniform random numbers into random numbers with distribution function \(F\).

title: Seminar 7: Continuous Random Variables. Normal Distribution
text:
3.2 Example: Exponential Distribution
Let \(X\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\). Its cumulative distribution function is
\[
F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x},
\qquad x\ge0.
\]
To generate \(X\), we solve \(u=1-e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\).
This gives
\[
x=-\frac1\lambda\ln(1-u).
\]
Hence, if \(U\sim U(0,1)\), then
\[
\boxed{
X=-\frac1\lambda\ln(1-U)
\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda).
}
\]
Since \(1-U\) has the same distribution as \(U\), we often write simply \(X=-\frac1\lambda\ln U\).


Show Python code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import expon, norm

np.random.seed(42)

n = 50000
lam = 2

# Uniform random numbers

# Transformations
X_exp = -(1 / lam) * np.log(1 - U)
X_norm = norm.ppf(U)

# Theoretical densities
x_exp = np.linspace(0, 4, 1000)
pdf_exp = expon.pdf(x_exp, scale=1 / lam)

x_norm = np.linspace(-4, 4, 1000)
pdf_norm = norm.pdf(x_norm)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

# Uniform
ax = axes[0]
ax.hist(U, bins=40, density=True, alpha=0.65)
ax.axhline(1, linestyle="--", linewidth=3)
ax.set_title("Uniform random numbers")
ax.text(
    0.5, 1.22,
    "U ~ Uniform(0,1)",
    ha="center",
    fontsize=13,
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", facecolor="white", edgecolor="gray")
)
ax.set_xlabel("u")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.35)

# Exponential

ax.hist(X_exp, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.65)
ax.plot(x_exp, pdf_exp, linewidth=3)
ax.set_title("Transformation to Exponential(2)")
ax.text(

# Normal

title: Seminar 11: Point Estimators and their Properties
text:
Suppose a random variable \(X\) describes some phenomenon of interest. Examples include

the height of a randomly selected person;
tomorrow’s stock return;
the lifetime of a battery;
the salary of a software engineer.

Usually, the probability distribution of \(X\) is unknown. Instead, we observe only a finite sample
\[
X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n.
\]
The purpose of inferential statistics is to use this sample to draw conclusions about the unknown probability distribution.


Show Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.image as mpimg

image = mpimg.imread("images/sample.jpg")

plt.figure(figsize=(14, 8))
plt.imshow(image)
plt.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











The fundamental object in mathematical statistics is a random sample. A random sample of size \(n\) is a collection of independent and identically distributed random variables
\[
X_1,\ldots,X_n,
\]
such that \(X_i \sim F_\theta\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), where \(\theta\in\Theta\) is an unknown parameter.
Notice that \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are random variables, not numbers. Only after the experiment is performed do we observe one realization
\[
x_1,\ldots,x_n.
\]
Inference is based entirely on these observations.


Show Python code

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from scipy import stats
from IPython.display import display, clear_output

A statistical model is a family of probability distributions
\[
\mathcal P
=
\{
P_\theta
:
\theta\in\Theta
\},
\]
indexed by an unknown parameter \(\theta\).
Examples include \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), where \(\theta=(\mu,\sigma^2)\), or \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), where \(\theta=p\). Notice that Parameters are constants. They are not random variables.
The goal of statistical inference is to estimate the unknown parameter \(\theta\) from the observed sample.



A statistic is any measurable function of the sample \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\). Formally,
\[
T
=
g(X_1,\ldots,X_n)
\]
for some measurable function \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\).
Since the observations are random variables, every statistic is itself a random variable.
Examples include \(\bar X\), \(S^2\), \(X_{(1)}\) and \(X_{(n)}\).

title: Seminar 11: Point Estimators and their Properties
text:
The fundamental object in mathematical statistics is a random sample. A random sample of size \(n\) is a collection of independent and identically distributed random variables
\[
X_1,\ldots,X_n,
\]
such that \(X_i \sim F_\theta\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), where \(\theta\in\Theta\) is an unknown parameter.
Notice that \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are random variables, not numbers. Only after the experiment is performed do we observe one realization
\[
x_1,\ldots,x_n.
\]
Inference is based entirely on these observations.

title: Seminar 11: Point Estimators and their Properties
text:
2.1 Sampling Distributions
Since every estimator is a random variable, it has its own probability distribution. The probability distribution of an estimator is called its sampling distribution.
For example, suppose $ X_1,,X_n N(,^2)$. Then the sample mean is itself a random variable satisfying
\[
\bar X
\sim
N\left(
\mu,
\frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\right).
\]
Notice that this distribution is not the same as the distribution of a single observation.

2.2 Standard Error
The standard error of an estimator is its standard deviation,
\[
SE(\widehat\theta)
=
\sqrt{
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)

title: Seminar 11: Point Estimators and their Properties
text:
2.3 Properties of Estimators

2.3.1 Unbiasedness
An estimator \(\widehat\theta\) is unbiased if
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat\theta)
=
0.
\]
Unbiasedness means that, on average, the estimator correctly estimates the true parameter.


2.3.2 Consistency
An estimator \(\widehat\theta_n\) is consistent if
\[
\widehat\theta_n
\overset{P}{\longrightarrow}
\theta.
\]
Consistency guarantees that, as the sample size grows, the estimator approaches the true parameter with high probability.


Show Python code

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

mu = 0
sigma = 3
sample_sizes = [5, 20, 100, 500]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    nrows=2,
    ncols=2,
    figsize=(12, 8),
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, n in zip(axes, sample_sizes):
    samples = rng.normal(
        loc=mu,
        scale=sigma,
        size=(number_of_simulations, n)
    )

    first_observation_estimator = samples[:, 0]
    sample_mean_estimator = samples.mean(axis=1)

    ax.hist(
        first_observation_estimator,
        bins=60,
        density=True,
        alpha=0.5,
        label="First observation"
    )

    ax.hist(
        sample_mean_estimator,
        bins=60,
        density=True,
        alpha=0.6,
        label="Sample mean"
    )

        x=mu,
        color="red",
        linestyle="--",
        linewidth=2
    )

    ax.set_title(f"Sample size n = {n}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Estimate")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

axes[0].legend()

    "Both Estimators Are Unbiased, but Only the Sample Mean Is Consistent",
    fontsize=15
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()











2.3.3 Asymptotic Normality
An estimator \(\widehat\theta_n\) is asymptotically normal if, for some constant \(V>0\),
\[
\sqrt n
(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,V).
\]
Asymptotic normality is one of the most important properties in statistical inference because it allows us to construct confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

Let \(X_1,\ldots, X_n\) be a sample. Sorting the observations gives \(X_{(1)}\le X_{(2)}\le\cdots\le X_{(n)}\), called the order statistics.

title: Seminar 11: Point Estimators and their Properties
text:
2.5 Mean Squared Error
The Mean Squared Error (MSE) measures the overall quality of an estimator. It is defined as
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\theta)
=
E[(\widehat\theta-\theta)^2].
\]
Using \(E[X^2]=\operatorname{Var}(X)+(E[X])^2\), one obtains the fundamental decomposition
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\theta)
=
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)
+
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat\theta)^2.
}
\]
This decomposition shows that a good estimator should have both small variance and small bias.

2.5.1 The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
When constructing an estimator, there are generally two competing objectives. On one hand, we would like the estimator to have small bias, so that its average value is close to the true parameter. On the other hand, we would like the estimator to have small variance, so that repeated estimates obtained from different samples are similar to one another.
Unfortunately, these two objectives often conflict.
Reducing the variance of an estimator may introduce additional bias, while removing the bias may increase its variability. This phenomenon is known as the bias-variance tradeoff, and it is one of the central ideas in modern statistics and machine learning. For this reason, unbiased estimators are not always preferable. In many applications, a slightly biased estimator with substantially smaller variance may produce more accurate estimates overall.


Show Python code

title: Seminar 6: Correlation and WLLN
text:
In many applications we are interested not only in the behavior of a single random variable, but also in the relationship between two random variables.
Covariance measures the direction of the linear relationship between two variables, while the correlation coefficient gives a normalized measure that always lies between \(-1\) and \(1\).
These quantities are fundamental throughout statistics, machine learning, finance, econometrics, and data analysis.

title: Seminar 6: Correlation and WLLN
text:
1.1 Properties of Covariance
For any random variables \(\xi,\eta,\xi_1,\xi_2\) and constants \(a,b\),

Symmetry
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\xi,\eta)
=
\operatorname{Cov}(\eta,\xi).
\]
Covariance with itself
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\xi,\xi)
=
\operatorname{Var}(\xi).
\]
Linearity
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(a\xi_1+b\xi_2,\eta)
=
a\,\operatorname{Cov}(\xi_1,\eta)
+
b\,\operatorname{Cov}(\xi_2,\eta).
\]
Independence implies zero covariance
If \(\xi\perp\!\!\!\perp\eta\), then
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\xi,\eta)=0.
\]
However, the converse is generally false: zero covariance does not imply independence.

title: Seminar 6: Correlation and WLLN
text:
1.2 Variance of a Sum
One of the most useful applications of covariance is computing variances of sums.
For any random variables \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\),
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i
\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\operatorname{Cov}(\xi_i,\xi_j).
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i
\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_i)
+
2\sum_{i<j}
\operatorname{Cov}(\xi_i,\xi_j).
\]
If the variables are independent, all covariance terms vanish, giving
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i
\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_i).
\]

title: Seminar 6: Correlation and WLLN
section: 2.1 Example: GDP Growth and Association Between Two Countries

title: Seminar 6: Correlation and WLLN
text:
3.1 Markov’s Inequality
Let \(\xi\ge0\) be a nonnegative random variable with finite expectation.
Then for every \(a>0\),
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(\xi\ge a)
\le
\frac{\mathbb E[\xi]}{a}.
}
\]
This inequality requires only the existence of the expectation and makes no assumptions on the distribution. Although often crude, it serves as the starting point for many stronger inequalities.

title: Seminar 6: Correlation and WLLN
text:
3.2 Chebyshev’s Inequality
Suppose \(\xi\) has finite expectation and finite variance.
Then for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P
\left(
|\xi-\mathbb E\xi|
\ge
\varepsilon
\right)
\le
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)}
{\varepsilon^2}.
}
\]
Unlike Markov’s inequality, Chebyshev’s inequality uses both the expectation and the variance.

title: Seminar 6: Correlation and WLLN
section: 4.1 Bernoulli Trials and the Interpretation of Probability
text:
4.1 Bernoulli Trials and the Interpretation of Probability
One of the most important consequences of the Weak Law of Large Numbers is that it provides a mathematical justification for interpreting probability as long-run relative frequency.
Suppose we repeat the same experiment independently many times. Let
\[
X_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the event occurs on trial } i,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\). Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[X_i]=p,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=p(1-p).
\]
Notice that \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\) is exactly the number of times the event occurred during the first \(n\) trials. Therefore,
\[
\overline X_n
=
\frac{\text{Number of successes}}
{\text{Number of trials}},
\]
which is precisely the empirical frequency (or relative frequency) of the event.
Applying the Weak Law of Large Numbers,
\[
\overline X_n
\xrightarrow{P}
p,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\mathbb P
\left(
\left|
\frac{\text{Number of successes}}{n}
-
p
\right|
>
\varepsilon
\right)
=0
\qquad
(\varepsilon>0).
}
\]
Thus, as the number of independent repetitions increases, the observed frequency of the event becomes arbitrarily close to its true probability with probability approaching one.
This result gives a rigorous mathematical foundation for the frequentist interpretation of probability:

The probability of an event is the limiting value of its relative frequency in a large number of independent repetitions of the same experiment.



Show Python code
p = 0.37
n = 5000

trials = np.random.binomial(1, p, size=n)
running_frequencies = np.cumsum(trials) / np.arange(1, n + 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.plot(running_frequencies, linewidth=2, label="Empirical frequency")
plt.axhline(p, linestyle="--", linewidth=3, label=f"True probability p = {p}")

plt.title("Weak Law of Large Numbers for Bernoulli trials")
plt.xlabel("Number of trials")
plt.ylabel("Relative frequency of success")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.show()

title: Seminar 10: CLT. Limit theorems
text:
There are several important notions describing how a sequence of random variables may converge.


We say that
\[
X_n
\overset{\mathrm{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow}
X
\]
if
\[
P\left(
\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\}
\right)=1.
\]
In words, the convergence holds for every outcome except possibly on a set of probability zero.


Consider the probability space \(\Omega=[0,1]\), equipped with the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal F=\mathcal B([0,1])\), and the Lebesgue probability measure. Define the sequence of random variables
\[
X_n(\omega)=\omega+\omega^n,
\qquad
\omega\in[0,1].
\]
We also define \(X(\omega)=\omega\). It follows that,
\[
X_n
\overset{\mathrm{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow}
X.
\]




We say that
\[
X_n
\overset{P}{\longrightarrow}
X
\]
if for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)
\longrightarrow0.
\]
This is the notion of convergence appearing in the Law of Large Numbers.


Let \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(n)\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
P(|X_n|>\varepsilon)
=
P(X_n>\varepsilon)
=
e^{-n\varepsilon}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Hence
\[
X_n
\overset{P}{\longrightarrow}
0.
\]




We say that
\[
X_n
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
X
\]
if
\[
F_{X_n}(x)\longrightarrow F_X(x)
\]
at every continuity point of \(F_X\).



In general, we have the following chain of implications:
\[
\boxed{
X_n
\overset{\mathrm{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow}
X
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X_n
\overset{P}{\longrightarrow}
X
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X_n
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
X.
}
\]
In general, the converse implications are false.



The various notions of convergence of random variables and random vectors are among the central concepts of modern probability theory.
They form the mathematical foundation of many advanced subjects, including Mathematical Statistics, Mathematical Finance and Stochastic Differential Equations.
Entire graduate courses are devoted to understanding the relationships between these different notions of convergence and learning the powerful theorems associated with them (Slutsky’s theorem, the Continuous Mapping Theorem, Skorokhod’s Representation Theorem, Prokhorov’s Theorem, and many others).
Fortunately, our goals in this course are much more modest.
Since this is an introductory course in inferential statistics, we only need to understand

the definitions of the main types of convergence;
how to interpret them intuitively;
where they appear in the Law of Large Numbers and the Central Limit Theorem.

title: Seminar 10: CLT. Limit theorems
text:
2.1 Poisson Limit Theorem
The Poisson distribution naturally appears as the limit of a binomial distribution when the number of trials is large while the probability of success is small.
Let \(X_n \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n,p_n)\), where
\[
n p_n \longrightarrow \lambda>0.
\]
Then for every fixed integer \(k\ge0\),
\[
\boxed{
\lim_{n\to\infty}
P(X_n=k)
=
\frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}.
}
\]
In other words,
\[
X_n
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda).
\]
This theorem explains why the Poisson distribution is widely used to model rare events.


Show Python code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from scipy import stats
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (9, 5)
plt.rcParams["axes.grid"] = True
plt.rcParams["grid.alpha"] = 0.25




Show Python code

sample_sizes = [10, 20, 100]

x_values = np.arange(0, 16)

    figsize=(20, 4),
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

for axis, sample_size in zip(axes, sample_sizes):

        p=success_probability
    )

    poisson_probabilities = stats.poisson.pmf(
        x_values,
        mu=lambda_parameter
    )

    axis.bar(
        x_values,

        alpha=0.6,
        label="Binomial"
    )

title: Seminar 10: CLT. Limit theorems
text:
2.2 Weak Law of Large Numbers
The Weak Law of Large Numbers states that sample averages become arbitrarily close to the population mean with high probability.
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed random variables satisfying
\[
E[X_i]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty.
\]
Define the sample sum \(S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\boxed{
P\left(
\left|
\frac{S_n}{n}-\mu
\right|
>\varepsilon
\right)
\longrightarrow0.
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac{S_n}{n}
\overset{P}{\longrightarrow}
\mu.
\]


Show Python code
success_probability = 0.3
epsilon = 0.05

# --------------------------------------------------
# Parameters
# --------------------------------------------------

number_of_paths = 100
maximum_sample_size = 2000

sample_sizes = np.arange(1, maximum_sample_size + 1)

# --------------------------------------------------
# Left figure: sample means
# --------------------------------------------------

samples = rng.binomial(
    n=1,
    p=success_probability,
    size=(number_of_paths, maximum_sample_size)
)

running_means = (
    np.cumsum(samples, axis=1)
    / sample_sizes
)

# --------------------------------------------------
# Right figure:
# P(|X̄_n-p|>ε)
# --------------------------------------------------

sample_sizes_probability = np.array([
    10,
    20,
    50,
    100,
    200,
    500,
    1000,
    2000,
    5000
])

number_of_repetitions = 20_000

for sample_size in sample_sizes_probability:

    sample_means = (
        rng.binomial(
            n=sample_size,
            p=success_probability,
            size=number_of_repetitions
        )
        / sample_size
    )

    estimated_probabilities.append(
        np.mean(

            ) > epsilon
        )
    )

)

# --------------------------------------------------

title: Seminar 10: CLT. Limit theorems
text:
2.3 Central Limit Theorem
Unlike the Law of Large Numbers, which describes convergence to the mean, the Central Limit Theorem describes the fluctuations around the mean.
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed random variables satisfying
\[
E[X_i]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2>0.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\frac{S_n-n\mu}
{\sigma\sqrt n}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1).
}
\]
The Central Limit Theorem is one of the most important results in probability and statistics since it explains why normal distributions appear so frequently in practice.


Show Python code
sample_sizes = [1, 2, 5, 100]
number_of_repetitions = 50_000

x_grid = np.linspace(-4, 6, 500)
normal_density = stats.norm.pdf(x_grid)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    nrows=1,
    ncols=len(sample_sizes),
    figsize=(20, 4.5),
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

for axis, sample_size in zip(axes, sample_sizes):

    sums = rng.gamma(
        shape=sample_size,
        scale=1,
        size=number_of_repetitions
    )

    standardized_sums = (
        sums - sample_size
    ) / np.sqrt(sample_size)

    axis.hist(
        standardized_sums,
        bins=70,
        density=True,
        alpha=0.65,
        label="Simulation"
    )

    axis.plot(
        x_grid,
        normal_density,
        linewidth=2,
        label=r"$N(0,1)$"
    )

    axis.set_xlim(-4, 6)
    axis.set_title(rf"$n={sample_size}$")
    axis.set_xlabel("$z$")

axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[0].legend()

plt.suptitle(
    "Central Limit Theorem for Exponential Random Variables",
    fontsize=16
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Seminar 10: CLT. Limit theorems
section: 4.1 Simulation: The Multidimensional Central Limit Theorem
text:
4.1 Simulation: The Multidimensional Central Limit Theorem
In this simulation, we illustrate how the multidimensional Central Limit Theorem works.
We generate independent random vectors \(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^2\), where each coordinate is sampled independently from the uniform distribution
\[
U(-\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3}).
\]
The interval is chosen so that
\[
E[X_i]=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(X_i)=
I_2,
\]
where \(I_2\) denotes the \(2\times2\) identity matrix.
For each value of \(n\), we compute the standardized sum
\[
Z_n
=
\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n}{\sqrt n},
\]
and generate many independent realizations of \(Z_n\). Each point in the scatter plot represents one realization of this random vector.
According to the Multidimensional Central Limit Theorem,
\[
Z_n
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,I_2),
\]
as \(n\rightarrow\infty\).


Show Python code
sample_sizes = [1, 2, 5, 20, 100]
number_of_repetitions = 15_000

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    nrows=1,
    ncols=len(sample_sizes),
    figsize=(20, 4),
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

for axis, sample_size in zip(axes, sample_sizes):
    sample_sums = np.zeros(
        (number_of_repetitions, 2)
    )

    for _ in range(sample_size):
        sample_sums += rng.uniform(
            low=-np.sqrt(3),
            high=np.sqrt(3),
            size=(number_of_repetitions, 2)
        )

    standardized_sums = (
        sample_sums / np.sqrt(sample_size)
    )

    axis.scatter(
        standardized_sums[:, 0],
        standardized_sums[:, 1],
        s=3,
        alpha=0.25
    )

    axis.set_title(rf"$n={sample_size}$")
    axis.set_xlim(-4, 4)
    axis.set_ylim(-4, 4)
    axis.set_aspect("equal")

axes[0].set_ylabel("$y$")

for axis in axes:
    axis.set_xlabel("$x$")

plt.suptitle(
    "Multidimensional CLT: A Square-Shaped Distribution Becomes Gaussian",
    fontsize=15
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
Suppose that \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) is a random sample from a parametric family of probability distributions \(\mathcal P=\left\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\right\}\), where

\(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r\) is the parameter space, and
\(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)^T\) is the unknown parameter vector.

The objective of parametric estimation is to construct a statistic
\[
\widehat\theta
=
\widehat\theta(X_1,\ldots,X_n)
\]
that provides a good approximation of the true parameter value.
One of the oldest and most intuitive estimation procedures is the Method of Moments (MOM), introduced by Karl Pearson (1894). Its central idea is extremely simple:

Replace unknown theoretical moments by their corresponding sample moments and solve the resulting system of equations for the unknown parameters.

Although modern statistics often favors Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), the method of moments remains an important estimation technique due to its simplicity, computational efficiency, and broad applicability.


The method of moments is based on the observation that many probability distributions are completely determined by their moments. Let \(X\) be a random variable.

The \(k\)-th raw (non-central) moment of \(X\) is defined by

\[
\mu_k'
=
\mathbb E[X^k],
\qquad
k=1,2,\ldots.
\]

The \(k\)-th central moment is defined by

\[
\mu_k
=
\mathbb E[(X-\mu)^k].
\]
The first central moments are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_1 &=0,\\
\mu_2 &=\operatorname{Var}(X),\\
\mu_3 &\text{ measures the asymmetry (skewness) of the distribution},\\
\mu_4 &\text{ is related to the kurtosis of the distribution}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Although central moments describe many important properties of a distribution, the Method of Moments is usually formulated in terms of raw moments, since they lead to simpler systems of equations.



For a parametric family \(\mathcal P=\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), each theoretical moment is a function of the unknown parameter, \(\mu_k'(\theta)=
\mathbb E_\theta[X^k]\).
For example, if \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[X]
&=\mu,
\\[1ex]
\mathbb E[X^2]
&=\mu^2+\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently, if the theoretical moments determine the unknown parameters uniquely, they may be used to estimate those parameters.



Since the population moments are unknown, they must be estimated using the observed sample.


Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be a random sample. The \(k\)-th sample raw moment is defined by
\[
\boxed{
M_k'
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
X_i^k.
}
\]
In particular, \(M_1'=\overline{X}\). Each sample moment is a statistic and therefore a random variable.



The fundamental justification for the Method of Moments follows directly from the Law of Large Numbers. Indeed, provided the \(k\)-th moment exists,
\[
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
X_i^k
\xrightarrow{P}
\mathbb E[X^k].
\]
Therefore, for sufficiently large samples,
\[
M_k'
\approx
\mu_k'.
\]
This observation motivates replacing unknown population moments by their empirical counterparts.




Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_r:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R\), be measurable functions such that \(\mathbb E_\theta[g_i(X)]\) exists for every parameter value. Here \(\theta \in \mathbb R^r\).
Define the theoretical quantities
\[
m_i(\theta)
:=
\mathbb E_\theta[g_i(X)],
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,r.
\]
The corresponding empirical quantities are
\[
\widehat m_i
:=
\frac1n
\sum_{j=1}^n
g_i(X_j).
\]
The Method of Moments estimates the parameter by solving the system
\[
\boxed{
m_i(\theta)
=
\widehat m_i,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,r.
}
\]
If this system admits a unique solution \(\widehat\theta\), then \(\widehat\theta\) is called the Method of Moments estimator (MME).


The functions \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) are called the moment functions (or estimating functions).
The classical Method of Moments corresponds to the particular choice
\[
g_i(x)=x^i,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,r.
\]
More general choices of the functions \(g_i\) lead to generalized moment-based estimation procedures, such as the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) used extensively in econometrics.




Let \(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)\), be an unknown parameter vector. The estimator is obtained as follows:

Compute the first \(r\) theoretical moments

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[X],
\;
\mathbb E_\theta[X^2],
\;
\ldots,
\;
\mathbb E_\theta[X^r].
\]

Compute the corresponding sample moments

\[
M_1',
\;
M_2',
\;
\ldots,
\;
M_r'.
\]

Solve the system

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[X^k]
=
M_k',
\qquad
k=1,\ldots,r.
\]

The solution is the Method of Moments estimator

\[
\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MOM}}.
\]
For many standard probability distributions, this system admits an explicit analytical solution. In more complicated models, numerical methods may be required.


Suppose \(X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), where both parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are unknown.
Since there are two unknown parameters, we equate the first two theoretical moments to the corresponding sample moments.
The first theoretical moment is \(\mathbb E[X]=\mu\), while the second theoretical moment is \(\mathbb E[X^2]=\mu^2+\sigma^2\).
The Method of Moments equations are therefore
\[
\mu
=
\overline X,
\qquad
\mu^2+\sigma^2
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
X_i^2.
\]
We obtain the Method of Moments estimators
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{MOM}}
=
\overline X,
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{MOM}}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\overline X)^2.
}
\]
Notice that the estimator of the variance is biased, since it uses the denominator \(n\) rather than \(n-1\). Nevertheless, it is consistent and coincides with the Maximum Likelihood Estimator for the variance of a normal distribution.

\mu_k'.
\]
This observation motivates replacing unknown population moments by their empirical counterparts.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_r:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R\), be measurable functions such that \(\mathbb E_\theta[g_i(X)]\) exists for every parameter value. Here \(\theta \in \mathbb R^r\).
Define the theoretical quantities
\[
m_i(\theta)
:=
\mathbb E_\theta[g_i(X)],
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,r.
\]
The corresponding empirical quantities are
\[
\widehat m_i
:=
\frac1n
\sum_{j=1}^n
g_i(X_j).
\]
The Method of Moments estimates the parameter by solving the system
\[
\boxed{
m_i(\theta)
=
\widehat m_i,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,r.
}
\]
If this system admits a unique solution \(\widehat\theta\), then \(\widehat\theta\) is called the Method of Moments estimator (MME).


The functions \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) are called the moment functions (or estimating functions).
The classical Method of Moments corresponds to the particular choice
\[
g_i(x)=x^i,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,r.
\]
More general choices of the functions \(g_i\) lead to generalized moment-based estimation procedures, such as the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) used extensively in econometrics.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
Let \(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)\), be an unknown parameter vector. The estimator is obtained as follows:

Compute the first \(r\) theoretical moments

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[X],
\;
\mathbb E_\theta[X^2],
\;
\ldots,
\;
\mathbb E_\theta[X^r].
\]

Compute the corresponding sample moments

\[
M_1',
\;
M_2',
\;
\ldots,
\;
M_r'.
\]

Solve the system

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[X^k]
=
M_k',
\qquad
k=1,\ldots,r.
\]

The solution is the Method of Moments estimator

\[
\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MOM}}.
\]
For many standard probability distributions, this system admits an explicit analytical solution. In more complicated models, numerical methods may be required.


Suppose \(X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), where both parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are unknown.
Since there are two unknown parameters, we equate the first two theoretical moments to the corresponding sample moments.
The first theoretical moment is \(\mathbb E[X]=\mu\), while the second theoretical moment is \(\mathbb E[X^2]=\mu^2+\sigma^2\).
The Method of Moments equations are therefore
\[
\mu
=
\overline X,
\qquad
\mu^2+\sigma^2
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
X_i^2.
\]
We obtain the Method of Moments estimators
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{MOM}}
=
\overline X,
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{MOM}}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\overline X)^2.
}
\]
Notice that the estimator of the variance is biased, since it uses the denominator \(n\) rather than \(n-1\). Nevertheless, it is consistent and coincides with the Maximum Likelihood Estimator for the variance of a normal distribution.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
section: 2.1 Consistency of the Method of Moments
text:
2.1 Consistency of the Method of Moments
Suppose that \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) is a random sample from a distribution depending on the unknown parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\).
Assume that the required population moments exist, and also, that the mapping
\[
\theta
\longmapsto
\left(
\mu_1'(\theta),
\ldots,
\mu_r'(\theta)
\right)
\]
is continuous, and it is one-to-one (identifiable).
Then the Method of Moments estimator satisfies
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MOM}}
\xrightarrow{P}
\theta_0.
}
\]

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
2.2 Asymptotic Normality
The consistency theorem may be strengthened considerably.
Assume that, additionally to the previous conditions, the inverse mapping \(m^{-1}\) can be extended to a function defined on all of \(\mathbb R^k\), and is continuously differentiable at every point of the set \(m(\Theta)\). Moreover, for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\) and every \(\theta\in\Theta\), the moment function satisfies \(0<\operatorname{Var}_\theta\!\left(g_i(X)\right)<+\infty\). Then,
\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MOM}}
-
\theta_0
\right)
\xrightarrow{d}
N
\left(
0,
\Sigma_{\mathrm{MOM}}
\right).
}
\]
Consequently, for sufficiently large samples,
\[
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MOM}}
\approx
N
\left(
\theta_0,
\frac1n
\Sigma_{\mathrm{MOM}}
\right).
\]

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
section: 2.3 Advantages of the Method of Moments
text:
2.3 Advantages of the Method of Moments

It is conceptually simple.
It often leads to explicit closed-form estimators.
It usually requires only elementary algebra.
It does not require optimization algorithms.
It is applicable even when the likelihood function is difficult to maximize.

For these reasons, the Method of Moments is frequently used to obtain initial parameter estimates for more sophisticated estimation procedures.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
section: 2.4 Limitations of the Method of Moments
text:
2.4 Limitations of the Method of Moments
Despite its simplicity, the Method of Moments has several important drawbacks.

It generally ignores much of the information contained in the probability distribution.
Different choices of moments may produce different estimators.
Method of Moments estimators are not usually efficient.
They may have larger variance than maximum likelihood estimators.
In some models, the resulting system of equations may not admit a unique solution.

Consequently, although the Method of Moments is often computationally convenient, it is generally statistically less efficient than Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
3.1 The Likelihood Function
Suppose first that \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x;\theta)\). Consider the sample \(X_1,\ldots,X_n \sim X\).
The likelihood function is a function of \(\theta\), defined as
\[
L(\theta)
=
L(\theta;x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
f(x_i;\theta).
\]

3.1.1 Discrete Case
If the observations come from a discrete distribution with probability mass function \(p(x;\theta)\), the likelihood function becomes
\[
L(\theta)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
p(x_i;\theta).
\]
Therefore, the definition of the likelihood is identical for continuous and discrete distributions; only the underlying probability function changes.


3.1.2 Interpretation of the Likelihood
The likelihood function should not be interpreted as the probability that the parameter equals a particular value. The parameter is not considered to be a random variable.
Instead, \(L(\theta)\) answers the following question:

Assuming that the parameter equals \(\theta\), how compatible is the observed sample with the statistical model?

Consequently,

larger values of \(L(\theta)\) indicate that the observed data are more compatible with the model,
smaller values indicate that the observed sample would be less likely under that parameter value.

The goal of maximum likelihood estimation is therefore to choose the parameter that maximizes the likelihood.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
3.2 The Log-Likelihood Function
The log-likelihood function is defined by
\[
\ell(\theta)
=
\log L(\theta).
\]
Using the identity \(\log(ab)=\log a+\log b\), the product becomes a sum,
\[
\boxed{
\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\log f(x_i;\theta).
}
\]
This transformation greatly simplifies differentiation and optimization. Notice that maximizing the likelihood and maximizing the log-likelihood always produce exactly the same estimator, since
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}
L(\theta)
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}
\ell(\theta).
\]

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
section: 3.3 Definition of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator
text:
3.3 Definition of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator
The Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) is the parameter value that maximizes the likelihood function.
Formally, a statistic \(\widehat\theta\) is called a maximum likelihood estimator if
\[
\boxed{
\widehat\theta
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta\in\Theta}
L(\theta).
}
\]
Equivalently, \(\widehat\theta=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta\in\Theta} \ell(\theta)\).
The observed numerical value of \(\widehat\theta\) is called the maximum likelihood estimate.

3.3.1 Computing the MLE
When the likelihood is differentiable, the maximum likelihood estimator is typically obtained in three steps.

Construct the likelihood function \(L(\theta)\).
Compute the log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta)\).
Differentiate and solve \(\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}=0\).

Finally, verify that the solution corresponds to a maximum by checking the second derivative or using other optimization arguments. For multi-parameter models, the same procedure is applied using partial derivatives with respect to each parameter.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
section: 3.4 Example: MLE for a Normal Distribution
text:
3.4 Example: MLE for a Normal Distribution
Suppose \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), where both parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are unknown.
The probability density function is
\[
f(x;\mu,\sigma^2)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\exp\left(
-
\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}
\right).
\]
The likelihood function is
\[
L(\mu,\sigma^2)
=
\left(
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\right)^n
\exp\left(
-
\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\mu)^2
\right).
\]
Taking logarithms,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2)
&=
\log L(\mu,\sigma^2)
\\[1ex]
&=
-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)
-\frac{n}{2}\log(\sigma^2)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\mu)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]


3.4.1 Step 1 — Estimate of the Mean
Differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to \(\mu\):
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mu}
=
\frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\mu).
\]
Setting the derivative equal to zero, which gives
\[
n\mu
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
X_i.
\]
Hence,
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=
\overline X
}
\]



3.4.2 Step 2 — Estimate of the Variance
Differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to \(\sigma^2\):
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2}
=
-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}
+
\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Setting this derivative equal to zero,
\[
-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}
+
\frac{1}{2(\sigma^2)^2}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\mu)^2
=
0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sigma^2
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Substituting \(\mu=\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\overline X\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(X_i-\overline X)^2
}
\]
Notice that \(\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}\) is a biased estimator of the population variance. Nevertheless, it is consistent, asymptotically normal, and asymptotically efficient. Moreover, for the normal distribution, it coincides with the Method of Moments estimator of the variance.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
4.1 Maximum Likelihood Equations
Since the maximum of a differentiable function is attained at a critical point, the maximum likelihood estimator usually satisfies
\[
\boxed{
U(\widehat\theta)=0.
}
\]
These equations are called the likelihood equations or score equations.
For a single parameter,
\[
\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}
{\partial\theta}
=
0,
\]
whereas for several parameters,
\[
\frac{\partial\ell(\theta)}
{\partial\theta_j}
=
0,
\qquad
j=1,\ldots,p.
\]
The solution of this system is the maximum likelihood estimator, provided that it corresponds to a maximum of the likelihood.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
4.2 Interpretation
The score function plays a role analogous to the derivative of an ordinary function.

If

\[
U(\theta)>0,
\]
the log-likelihood is increasing.

If

\[
U(\theta)<0,
\]
the log-likelihood is decreasing.

If

\[
U(\theta)=0,
\]
the log-likelihood has a stationary point, which may correspond to a local maximum, a local minimum, or a saddle point.
Consequently, solving
\[
U(\theta)=0
\]
is the first step in computing the maximum likelihood estimator.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
5.1 Theorem
Suppose that the regularity conditions allowing differentiation under the integral sign are satisfied.
Then,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_\theta
\!\left[
U(\theta)
\right]
=
0.
}
\]
In other words, the score function is an unbiased estimating function.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
5.2 Proof
Recall that
\[
U(\theta)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\ell(\theta)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\log L(\theta).
\]
For a random sample,
\[
L(\theta)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
f(X_i;\theta),
\]
and therefore
\[
U(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\log f(X_i;\theta).
\]
Hence,
\[
\mathbb E_\theta[U(\theta)]
=
n
\,
\mathbb E_\theta
\!\left[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\log f(X;\theta)
\right].
\]
Since
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\log f(x;\theta)
=
\frac{1}{f(x;\theta)}
\frac{\partial f(x;\theta)}
{\partial\theta},
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_\theta
\!\left[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\log f(X;\theta)
\right]
&=
\int
\frac{1}{f(x;\theta)}
\frac{\partial f(x;\theta)}
{\partial\theta}
f(x;\theta)
\,dx
\\[1ex]
&=
\int
\frac{\partial f(x;\theta)}
{\partial\theta}
\,dx
\\[1ex]
&=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\int
f(x;\theta)
\,dx
\\[1ex]
&=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(1)
\\[1ex]
&=
0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E_\theta
\!\left[
U(\theta)
\right]
=
0.
}
\]

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
5.3 Remark
The proof relies on the ability to interchange differentiation and integration,
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\int
f(x;\theta)\,dx
=
\int
\frac{\partial f(x;\theta)}
{\partial\theta}
\,dx,
\]
which is guaranteed under suitable regularity conditions.
These assumptions are satisfied for most classical parametric families encountered in practice.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
5.4 Corollary
Since
\[
\mathbb E_\theta[U(\theta)]
=
0,
\]
the variance of the score function is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(U(\theta))
=
\mathbb E_\theta
\!\left[
U(\theta)^2
\right].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
I(\theta)
=
\operatorname{Var}(U(\theta))
=
\mathbb E_\theta
\!\left[
U(\theta)^2
\right],
}
\]
which is known as the Information Equality.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
6.1 Definition
For a one-dimensional parameter,
\[
\boxed{
J(\theta)
=
-
\frac{\partial^2\ell(\theta)}
{\partial\theta^2}.
}
\]
The quantity
\[
J(\theta)
\]
is called the observed Fisher information.
For vector parameters,
\[
\boxed{
J(\theta)
=
-
\nabla_\theta^2
\ell(\theta),
}
\]
that is, the negative Hessian matrix of the log-likelihood.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
6.2 Interpretation
The observed Fisher information measures the local curvature of the log-likelihood.
A sharply peaked likelihood has large curvature and therefore contains more information about the unknown parameter.
Conversely, a flat likelihood changes very little as the parameter varies, making estimation more difficult.
Consequently,

large Fisher information corresponds to more precise estimation,
small Fisher information corresponds to greater uncertainty.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
7.1 Definition
The Fisher information is
\[
\boxed{
I(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta
\left[
J(\theta)
\right]
=
-
\mathbb E_\theta
\left[
\frac{\partial^2\ell(\theta)}
{\partial\theta^2}
\right].
}
\]
For vector parameters,
\[
\boxed{
I(\theta)
=
-
\mathbb E_\theta
\left[
\nabla_\theta^2
\ell(\theta)
\right].
}
\]
Unlike the observed information,
\[
J(\theta),
\]
the Fisher information depends only on the statistical model and not on the observed sample.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
7.2 Information Equality
Under suitable regularity conditions,
\[
\boxed{
I(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta
\left[
U(\theta)^2
\right].
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
I(\theta)
=
\operatorname{Var}
\bigl(
U(\theta)
\bigr),
}
\]
since
\[
\mathbb E_\theta
\left[
U(\theta)
\right]
=
0.
\]
Thus, the Fisher information may be computed either from the expected curvature of the log-likelihood or from the variance of the score function.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
7.3 Why Is Fisher Information Important?
Fisher information quantifies the amount of information that the observed sample contains about the unknown parameter.
It plays a central role throughout mathematical statistics.
In particular,

it determines the asymptotic variance of the maximum likelihood estimator,
it appears in the Cramér–Rao Lower Bound,
it characterizes asymptotic efficiency,
and it provides the basis for likelihood ratio, score, and Wald hypothesis tests.

For these reasons, Fisher information is one of the most fundamental concepts in statistical inference.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
7.4 Summary
The differential quantities associated with the likelihood are








Quantity
Definition
Purpose




Score
\[U(\theta)=\dfrac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta}\]
Finds stationary points


Observed Fisher Information
\[J(\theta)=-\dfrac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\theta^2}\]
Measures local curvature


Fisher Information
\[I(\theta)=\mathbb E[J(\theta)]\]
Measures information contained in the model



Together, these quantities form the mathematical foundation of maximum likelihood estimation.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.1 Consistency of the MLE
An estimator \(\widehat{\theta}_n\) is called consistent for \(\theta_0\) if
\[
\widehat{\theta}_n
\xrightarrow{P}
\theta_0.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\mathbb P_{\theta_0}
\left(
\left\|
\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0
\right\|>\varepsilon
\right)
\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Thus, consistency means that the estimator becomes arbitrarily close to the true parameter with high probability as the sample size increases.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.2 Consistency Theorem for the MLE
Let
\[
X_1,\ldots,X_n
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
f(x;\theta_0),
\]
where \(\theta_0\) is the true parameter value.
Under suitable regularity and identifiability conditions,
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\xrightarrow{P}
\theta_0.
}
\]
The key idea is that the normalized log-likelihood satisfies
\[
\frac1n\ell_n(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
\log f(X_i;\theta)
\xrightarrow{P}
\mathbb E_{\theta_0}
\left[
\log f(X;\theta)
\right].
\]
The limiting objective function is maximized at the true parameter \(\theta_0\).
Therefore, the maximizer of the empirical log-likelihood converges to the maximizer of its population counterpart.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.3 Identifiability
A statistical model is called identifiable if distinct parameter values correspond to distinct probability distributions.
Formally,
\[
P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta_1=\theta_2.
\]
Equivalently, if
\[
f(x;\theta_1)=f(x;\theta_2)
\]
for almost every \(x\), then
\[
\theta_1=\theta_2.
\]
Identifiability is necessary for consistent estimation: if two different parameter values generate exactly the same distribution, no estimator can distinguish between them.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
section: 8.4 Why Is the Expected Log-Likelihood Maximized at the Truth?
text:
8.4 Why Is the Expected Log-Likelihood Maximized at the Truth?
Define the population criterion
\[
Q(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_{\theta_0}
\left[
\log f(X;\theta)
\right].
\]
Then
\[
Q(\theta_0)-Q(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_{\theta_0}
\left[
\log
\frac{f(X;\theta_0)}
{f(X;\theta)}
\right].
\]
The right-hand side is the Kullback–Leibler divergence
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}
\left(
P_{\theta_0}\,\|\,P_\theta
\right).
\]
Since
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}
\left(
P_{\theta_0}\,\|\,P_\theta
\right)
\geq 0,
\]
we obtain
\[
Q(\theta_0)\geq Q(\theta).
\]
Under identifiability, equality holds only when
\[
\theta=\theta_0.
\]
Hence, the expected log-likelihood is uniquely maximized at the true parameter.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.5 Asymptotic Normality of the MLE
Consistency alone states that the estimator converges to the true parameter.
To perform inference, we also need to know the rate of convergence and the approximate distribution of the estimation error.
Under suitable regularity conditions,
\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0
\right)
\xrightarrow{d}
N
\left(
0,
I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}
\right),
}
\]
where \(I_1(\theta_0)\) is the Fisher information contained in one observation.
Equivalently, if
\[
I_n(\theta_0)
=
nI_1(\theta_0),
\]
then for large \(n\),
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\approx
N
\left(
\theta_0,
I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}
\right).
}
\]

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.6 Derivation from the Score Equation
The MLE satisfies the score equation
\[
U_n(\widehat{\theta})=0.
\]
Expand the score around the true parameter \(\theta_0\):
\[
0
=
U_n(\theta_0)
+
U_n'(\widetilde{\theta})
\left(
\widehat{\theta}-\theta_0
\right),
\]
where \(\widetilde{\theta}\) lies between \(\widehat{\theta}\) and \(\theta_0\).
Therefore,
\[
\sqrt n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}-\theta_0
\right)
=
-
\left[
\frac1n
U_n'(\widetilde{\theta})
\right]^{-1}
\frac{U_n(\theta_0)}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Now,
\[
\frac{U_n(\theta_0)}{\sqrt n}
\xrightarrow{d}
N
\left(
0,
I_1(\theta_0)
\right)
\]
by the Central Limit Theorem, while
\[
-\frac1n
U_n'(\widetilde{\theta})
\xrightarrow{P}
I_1(\theta_0)
\]
by the Law of Large Numbers and consistency.
Hence,
\[
\sqrt n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}-\theta_0
\right)
\xrightarrow{d}
N
\left(
0,
I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}
\right).
\]

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.7 Vector-Valued Parameters
If
\[
\theta\in\mathbb R^p,
\]
then the asymptotic distribution becomes multivariate:
\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0
\right)
\xrightarrow{d}
N_p
\left(
0,
I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}
\right).
}
\]
Here,
\[
I_1(\theta_0)
\]
is the Fisher information matrix for one observation.
Thus, for large samples,
\[
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\approx
N_p
\left(
\theta_0,
\frac1n
I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}
\right).
\]

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.8 Estimated Asymptotic Variance
The true parameter \(\theta_0\) is unknown, so the Fisher information is usually evaluated at the MLE.
Thus,
\[
\operatorname{Avar}
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right)
\approx
I_n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right)^{-1}.
\]
Alternatively, one may use the observed Fisher information,
\[
J_n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right)
=
-
\ell_n''
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right)
=
J_n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right)^{-1}.
}
\]
The square root of this quantity is called the estimated standard error of the MLE.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.9 Asymptotic Efficiency
An estimator is called asymptotically efficient if its asymptotic variance attains the smallest possible variance among regular estimators.
For a scalar parameter, the Cramér–Rao Lower Bound suggests that the smallest possible asymptotic variance is
\[
\frac{1}{nI_1(\theta_0)}.
\]
Since
\[
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\approx
N
\left(
\theta_0,
\frac{1}{nI_1(\theta_0)}
\right),
\]
the MLE attains this lower bound asymptotically.
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Avar}
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right)
=
\frac{1}{nI_1(\theta_0)}.
}
\]
In this sense, the MLE is asymptotically efficient.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.10 Important Remark on Efficiency
The MLE need not be unbiased for finite \(n\).
It may also fail to attain the Cramér–Rao Lower Bound exactly in small samples.
Asymptotic efficiency means that, as \(n\to\infty\),
\[
n\operatorname{Var}
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right)
\longrightarrow
I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}.
\]
Thus, the efficiency of the MLE is primarily a large-sample property.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.11 Invariance Property of the MLE
One of the most useful properties of maximum likelihood estimation is its invariance under transformations.
Suppose that
\[
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\]
is the MLE of \(\theta\), and let
\[
\eta=g(\theta)
\]
be a transformation of the parameter.
Then the MLE of \(\eta\) is
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=
g
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right).
}
\]
Thus, to estimate a function of the parameter, one simply applies the same function to the MLE.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.12 Invariance Theorem
Let
\[
\widehat{\theta}
\in
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta\in\Theta}
L(\theta).
\]
Suppose that
\[
\eta=g(\theta).
\]
Then an MLE of \(\eta\) is
\[
\widehat{\eta}
=
g(\widehat{\theta}).
\]
If \(g\) is one-to-one, the result follows immediately by reparameterizing the likelihood.
If \(g\) is not one-to-one, the profile likelihood for \(\eta\) is defined by
\[
L^*(\eta)
=
\sup_{\theta:g(\theta)=\eta}
L(\theta).
\]
Since \(\widehat{\theta}\) maximizes \(L(\theta)\), the value
\[
g(\widehat{\theta})
\]
maximizes \(L^*(\eta)\).

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
8.13 Example of Invariance
Suppose that
\[
X_1,\ldots,X_n
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
N(\mu,\sigma^2),
\]
and that the MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is
\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
(X_i-\overline X)^2.
\]
Since
\[
\sigma
=
\sqrt{\sigma^2},
\]
the invariance property implies that the MLE of \(\sigma\) is
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\sigma}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=
\sqrt{
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
(X_i-\overline X)^2
}.
}
\]
No separate maximization is required.

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
section: 8.14 Summary of the Main MLE Properties
text:
8.14 Summary of the Main MLE Properties
Under suitable regularity conditions, the maximum likelihood estimator satisfies
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\xrightarrow{P}
\theta_0
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0
\right)
\xrightarrow{d}
N
\left(
0,
I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}
\right).
}
\]
Consequently, the MLE is asymptotically efficient.
Moreover, for any transformation
\[
\eta=g(\theta),
\]
the corresponding MLE is
\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=
g
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\right).
}
\]
These properties can be summarized as follows:







Property
Mathematical statement




Consistency
\(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}\xrightarrow{P}\theta_0\)


Asymptotic normality
\(\sqrt n(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,I_1(\theta_0)^{-1})\)


Asymptotic efficiency
\(\operatorname{Avar}(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}})=I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}\)


Invariance
\(\widehat{g(\theta)}_{\mathrm{MLE}}=g(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}})\)

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
9.1 Population Quantiles
Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with cumulative distribution function
\[
F(x).
\]

9.1.1 Definition
For a probability level
\[
0<p<1,
\]
the \(p\)-th population quantile is the value
\[
\boxed{
q_p
=
F^{-1}(p),
}
\]
that satisfies
\[
\boxed{
F(q_p)=p.
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
P(X\le q_p)=p.
}
\]
Thus, a proportion \(p\) of the population lies below the quantile \(q_p\).

title: Seminar 12: MLE & Method of Moments
text:
9.2 Examples
Some commonly used quantiles are



Probability
Quantile
Interpretation




\(0.25\)
First quartile (\(Q_1\))
25% of observations lie below


\(0.50\)

Half of the observations lie below


\(0.75\)

75% of observations lie below

Top 10% begin above this value


\(0.95\)

Frequently used in risk analysis


\(0.99\)
99th percentile
